Subject: Trident Health: initial follow-up + proposed reliability tests

Hi Alice —

Great meeting this morning — thanks for walking us through the Trident inference requirements and the uptime constraints for the radiology pipeline. I wanted to capture the short list of next actions and clarify the two reliability vectors you asked us to validate against the hyperscaler baseline:

1) High-throughput steady-state: 200 concurrent inference streams, p90 latency target <= 250ms for 512-token requests
2) Failover/region outage: seamless routing to secondary region with max additional latency of 150ms and no more than 0.2% error spike in the first 5 minutes
3) Throttling behavior: rate-limit signal propagation to downstream systems and graceful 429 handling

Requests from your side that will help our next evaluation:
- Can you share the anonymized traffic spike pattern (CSV) for a typical week and a 1-hour outage window?
- Do you have an internal SLO definition for acceptable error budget burn that we should use for comparisons?

I've attached a one-page SLO comparison template and a short checklist we plan to run in our dedicated eval; Marissa (cc'd) will coordinate scheduling and the test harness. Proposed timeline: run a controlled bakeoff early next week (Mon/Tue), then share a short recording and the raw test logs.

If that works, I'll lock in a 60-minute slot for the bakeoff prep with your infra lead.

Best,

From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>

Alice — thanks for the quick reply and the SLO detail. Quick notes on the two technical questions so Kenji has context before the prep call:

1) KV cache & session context during failover
- For our hosted and dedicated modes we maintain per-request KV caches on the serving nodes. During an inter-region failover we do an index-style fallback: we route new requests to the secondary region and supply the best-effort prefix cache when available. We do not attempt transparent cross-region live replication of the KV cache because of RTO/consistency tradeoffs; instead we rely on request-level checkpoints and short-lived prefix caching to limit repetition. Practically, that means a small amount of token re-generation for long-running chats (usually < 2-3 tokens per request in our tests) unless the client provides an explicit session checkpoint.

2) Cold-starts and autoscaling for Dedicated
- Dedicated pools have a warm standby buffer and configurable burst capacity. Cold-starts (if you exhaust both warm capacity and burst) add an extra 350–700ms for the first request while kernels and memory maps load depending on model size. We've included a quantized model profile in the attached CSV that shows median cold-starts across sizes. If you want <250ms tail during autoscale events we recommend the "reserve burst" setting at 20% for your pool.

Next steps I propose:
- Kenji + Marissa + Connor + one Redwood infra engineer (Logan) on a 45-minute prep call tomorrow 10:00am PT to lock test parameters and produce the test script.
- We will run: steady-state ramp (0 -> 200 concurrent), two short bursts (x2 traffic for 7m), a simulated AZ-region failover (cut primary, route to secondary), and a throttling window that triggers 429s for a controlled 10-minute interval.

Connor will send a calendar invite if that time works.

Thanks,
Marissa Cole
Solutions Engineering — Redwood Inference
marissa_cole@redwood.com
